theory.what: OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) is a link-state routing protocol standardized as RFC 2328. Unlike distance-vector protocols (RIP, EIGRP) that share full routing tables with neighbours, OSPF floods Link-State Advertisements (LSAs) to all routers in an area, building a complete topological map called the Link-State Database (LSDB). Every OSPF router then runs Dijkstra's Shortest Path First (SPF) algorithm independently on that LSDB to compute the shortest path tree to every destination. The result is a loop-free, metric-based routing table where every router converges on the same topology picture. OSPF supports VLSM, CIDR, authentication (MD5/SHA), and classless routing natively. It uses cost as its metric, calculated as the reference bandwidth (100 Mbps by default) divided by the interface bandwidth, giving administrators fine-grained control over path selection.
theory.why: OSPF is the dominant interior gateway protocol (IGP) in enterprise and service provider networks for several reasons. First, its fast convergence: when a link fails, OSPF detects the change within seconds (Hello timer: 10s, Dead timer: 40s) and floods the update network-wide, triggering only affected routers to re-run SPF rather than recalculating everything. Second, its hierarchical design through areas dramatically reduces routing table size and SPF computation for larger networks. Third, OSPF provides loop-free routing intrinsically. Fourth, OSPF is vendor-interoperable. Fifth, LSA types enable advanced capabilities such as route summarization, external route injection, and NSSA partial external injection. Mastering OSPF is required for CCNA, CCNP, JNCIA, and virtually all network engineering certifications and roles.
theory.how: OSPF operation follows a structured five-phase process. Phase 1 — Neighbour Discovery: Routers send Hello packets every 10 seconds (default) to multicast 224.0.0.5 (AllSPFRouters) on broadcast media. Phase 2 — LSA Exchange: Once neighbours reach the 2-Way state, they proceed through ExStart/Exchange states to compare their LSDB summaries. A designated router (DR) and backup designated router (BDR) are elected on broadcast networks to reduce LSA flooding from O(n²) to O(n). Phase 3 — Database Synchronisation: Routers send Link-State Request (LSR) packets and receive Link-State Update (LSU) packets. Phase 4 — SPF Computation: Each router independently runs Dijkstra's algorithm on its LSDB to construct a Shortest Path Tree. Phase 5 — Ongoing Maintenance: Hello packets continue every 10 seconds. OSPF neighbour states: Down → Attempt (NBMA only) → Init → 2-Way → ExStart → Exchange → Loading → Full.
theory.when: Use OSPF in any network that needs fast convergence, hierarchical scaling, and vendor independence. Typical scenarios include: enterprise campus networks, ISP backbone networks, data centre leaf-spine topologies, multi-vendor environments, and MPLS LDP/TE environments. Use OSPF Area 0 for the backbone transit core, standard areas for leaf connectivity, stub areas to reduce LSA flooding, and NSSA to inject limited external routes. Avoid OSPF in flat networks exceeding 500 routers within a single area, in networks with frequent flapping links, or when sub-second convergence is required (consider IS-IS instead).
key_concepts: Area hierarchy (Backbone Area 0, standard, stub, NSSA, totally stubby)
LSA Types 1-7 (Router, Network, Summary, ASBR-Summary, AS-External, NSSA)
Router ID selection and manual configuration
ABR (Area Border Router) and ASBR (AS Boundary Router)
Virtual links for connecting discontinuous Area 0
Graceful restart / NSF for hitless upgrades
theory.configuration:
! OSPF configuration — three-area design
router ospf 1
 router-id 1.1.1.1
 network 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.3 area 0
 network 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 area 1
 network 172.16.0.0 0.0.255.255 area 2
 passive-interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 auto-cost reference-bandwidth 10000
 area 1 range 192.168.0.0 255.255.0.0
 area 2 stub no-summary
 timers throttle spf 50 200 10000
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip ospf cost 10
 ip ospf hello-interval 10
 ip ospf dead-interval 40
 ip ospf priority 10
 ip ospf authentication message-digest
 ip ospf message-digest-key 1 md5 OSPFSecret123
theory.worked_examples:
**Worked Example 1: Setting Up OSPF in a Three-Area Network**
A company has three sites connected via WAN links. The core site uses Area 0, with two remote sites in Area 1 and Area 2.

R1 (Core — Area 0 and ABR):
  router ospf 1
   router-id 1.1.1.1
   network 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.3 area 0       ! WAN to R2
   network 10.0.0.4 0.0.0.3 area 0       ! WAN to R3
   network 172.16.0.0 0.0.255.255 area 0  ! Core LAN
   area 1 range 192.168.0.0 255.255.0.0   ! Summarize Area 1
   area 2 range 172.17.0.0 255.255.0.0    ! Summarize Area 2

R2 (Remote Site 1 — Area 1):
  router ospf 1
   router-id 2.2.2.2
   network 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.3 area 0       ! WAN link must be Area 0
   network 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 area 1
   network 192.168.2.0 0.0.0.255 area 1
   passive-interface GigabitEthernet0/1

R3 (Remote Site 2 — Totally Stubby Area 2):
  router ospf 1
   router-id 3.3.3.3
   area 2 stub no-summary
   network 10.0.0.4 0.0.0.3 area 0
   network 172.17.1.0 0.0.0.255 area 2

Verification:
- show ip ospf neighbor → all three routers should show Full state
- show ip route ospf on R2 → should show default route + Area 2 subnets via R1
- show ip route on R1 → should show 192.168.0.0/16 (summarized), not individual /24s

**Worked Example 2: Diagnosing OSPF Neighbour Issues**
Symptom: Two routers connected directly won't form OSPF adjacency.

Step 1 — Check L1/L2: ping 10.0.0.2 source 10.0.0.1
Step 2 — Show ip ospf interface Gi0/0: confirm network type, cost, and state
Step 3 — Show ip ospf neighbor:
- Stuck in INIT: mismatched subnet mask or area ID
- Stuck in 2-WAY: waiting for DR/BDR election
- Stuck in EXSTART/EXCHANGE: MTU mismatch! Fix with 'ip mtu 1500' on both sides and 'clear ip ospf process'

**Worked Example 3: Cost Manipulation**
To prefer a backup link over the primary:
  interface GigabitEthernet0/1
   ip ospf cost 100    ! Higher cost = less preferred
Default cost for 100Mbps is 1; setting it to 100 makes the link strongly disfavoured.
theory.summary:
**Key Takeaways:**
• OSPF is a link-state IGP using Dijkstra's SPF algorithm on a complete topology map (LSDB)
• Hello/Dead timers (10s/40s) maintain neighbour relationships; failure triggers fast convergence
• Areas reduce SPF computation — Area 0 is the backbone that all other areas connect to
• OSPF cost = reference bandwidth / interface bandwidth; manipulate cost for traffic engineering
• DR/BDR election reduces flooding on broadcast networks from O(n²) to O(n)
• Set router-id manually, use passive interfaces on access ports, and tune SPF timers for faster convergence
• OSPFv3 runs on IPv6 with per-link (not per-subnet) semantics

**Best Practice:** Configure OSPF on point-to-point links where possible (no DR/BDR election overhead, faster convergence).
troubleshooting: show ip ospf neighbor [detail] — Verify neighbours have reached Full state
show ip ospf database — Inspect LSDB contents per LSA type
show ip ospf interface [name] — Check timers, cost, state, DR/BDR
show ip route ospf — Verify OSPF-learned routes in RIB
show ip protocols — Confirm OSPF process configuration
show ip ospf — Display process ID, RID, SPF stats, areas
debug ip ospf adj — Troubleshoot neighbour adjacency issues in real time
debug ip ospf packet — Analyse incoming/outgoing OSPF packets
clear ip ospf process — Force full OSPF restart (use with caution!)

theory.what: BGP (Border Gateway Protocol), defined in RFC 4271, is the path-vector routing protocol that interconnects the autonomous systems (ASes) forming the global internet. Unlike IGPs that care about the lowest-cost path, BGP is a policy-driven protocol where operators select paths based on business relationships and traffic engineering goals expressed through path attributes. BGP operates over TCP (port 179), ensuring reliable incremental updates. Each BGP route carries AS_PATH, NEXT_HOP, LOCAL_PREF, MULTI_EXIT_DISC (MED), and ORIGIN attributes. The global BGP routing table now exceeds 1 million IPv4 prefixes and 200,000 IPv6 prefixes.
theory.why: BGP is the protocol that makes the internet function. Every ISP, cloud provider (AWS, Azure, GCP), CDN (Cloudflare, Akamai), and large enterprise with multi-homed connectivity runs BGP. BGP enables: (1) multi-homed internet connectivity with traffic engineering using Local Pref and MED; (2) MPLS Layer 3 VPNs and EVPN fabrics; (3) cloud connectivity via Direct Connect and ExpressRoute; (4) fine-grained policy control through path attributes and communities that no IGP can match. Understanding BGP is critical for preventing blackholing and route leaks.
theory.how: BGP operation: Phase 1 — Session Establishment over TCP port 179 with OPEN messages (AS number, Hold Time, capabilities). Phase 2 — Initial UPDATE exchange of all feasible routes. Phase 3 — Incremental updates only after initial exchange. Phase 4 — Best Path Selection (10-step process): Weight → Local Pref → Local Origin → AS Path length → Origin → MED → eBGP/iBGP → IGP metric to next-hop → Age → Router ID. eBGP runs between ASes (TTL=1, AS_PATH loop prevention). iBGP runs within an AS (requires full mesh or route reflectors, split-horizon rules).
theory.when: Deploy BGP for: multi-homed internet connectivity, ISP peering at IXPs, cloud on-ramp (AWS Direct Connect, Azure ExpressRoute), data centre EVPN/VXLAN fabrics (RFC 7938), MPLS VPNs, and large enterprise WANs. Do NOT use BGP for simple internal routing where an IGP suffices — BGP adds complexity, slower convergence (30-90s default), and higher operational overhead.
key_concepts: eBGP (External BGP): between ASes, TTL=1, AS_PATH loop prevention
iBGP (Internal BGP): within AS, requires full mesh or route reflectors
Route Reflector (RR): scales iBGP from O(n²) to O(n)
AS_PATH attribute: sequence of AS numbers for loop detection and path length
Local Preference (LOCAL_PREF): 32-bit integer, higher preferred, controls outbound exit
Multi-Exit Discriminator (MED): 32-bit metric, lower preferred, influences inbound selection
BGP Communities: 32-bit tags for inter-AS signalling (NO_EXPORT, NO_ADVERTISE, LOCAL_AS)
Prefix filtering with prefix-lists, AS_PATH access-lists, route-maps
BGP convergence: ~90s by default; accelerated via BFD and Fast External Failover
Multiprotocol BGP (MP-BGP): VPNv4, IPv6, EVPN address families
BGP PIC: Prefix Independent Convergence for fast failover
BGP Flowspec: DDoS mitigation via route filtering
Graceful restart / NSF: hitless BGP session restart
theory.configuration:
! eBGP multi-homing configuration
router bgp 65001
 bgp router-id 10.0.0.1
 bgp log-neighbor-changes
 neighbor 203.0.113.1 remote-as 65002
 neighbor 203.0.113.1 description PRIMARY-ISP
 neighbor 203.0.113.1 ebgp-multihop 2
 neighbor 203.0.113.1 update-source Loopback0
 neighbor 203.0.113.1 password BGPSecureKey
 neighbor 203.0.113.1 timers 10 30
 neighbor 198.51.100.1 remote-as 65003
 neighbor 198.51.100.1 description BACKUP-ISP
 neighbor 198.51.100.1 password BGPSecureKey2
 network 10.0.0.0 mask 255.255.0.0
 network 192.168.0.0 mask 255.255.0.0
 route-map SET-LOCAL-PREF permit 10
  set local-preference 150
 neighbor 203.0.113.1 route-map SET-LOCAL-PREF in
 ip prefix-list ALLOWED permit 10.0.0.0/8 le 24
 neighbor 203.0.113.1 prefix-list ALLOWED in
 neighbor 203.0.113.1 prefix-list ALLOWED out
theory.worked_examples:
**Worked Example 1: Multi-Homed BGP with Traffic Engineering**
A company has two ISP connections — ISP-A (AS 65002) and ISP-B (AS 65003). They advertise prefix 203.0.113.0/24.

Goal: Prefer ISP-A for outbound and inbound traffic; ISP-B is backup.

Configuration:
- On ISP-A neighbour: apply route-map SET-LOCAL-PREF in (set local-preference 150)
- On ISP-B neighbour: apply route-map PREPEND-AS out (set as-path prepend 65001 65001 65001)

Outbound: Traffic leaves via ISP-A (LOCAL_PREF 150 > 100 default)
Inbound: Internet prefers ISP-A because ISP-B's path is longer (65001 65001 65001 65001 vs just 65001)
Failover: If ISP-A fails, BGP withdraws routes and traffic shifts to ISP-B automatically

**Worked Example 2: Diagnosing BGP Session Issues**
Symptom: BGP session stuck in Idle state.

Step 1 — ping peer source Loopback0 (TCP reachability)
Step 2 — nc -zv peer 179 (verify TCP port 179 open)
Step 3 — show run | section router bgp (verify remote-as on both sides)
Step 4 — show ip bgp summary (check state: Idle(Pfx)=prefix filter, Active=TCP issue, Idle(NoMem)=memory)
Step 5 — enable 'bgp log-neighbor-changes' for detailed state transitions

**Worked Example 3: BGP Community-Based Route Filtering**
A provider wants to prevent Customer A's routes from reaching Customer B (competitor).

Customer A tags routes: set community 65000:100 + send-community
Provider filters: ip community-list standard NO-CUST-B permit 65000:100
Provider applies: route-map FILTER-IN (match community NO-CUST-B) on Customer B's neighbour inbound.
Routes matching community 65000:100 are not sent to Customer B.
theory.summary:
**Key Takeaways:**
• BGP is a path-vector protocol making policy-based routing decisions using path attributes
• eBGP between ASes; iBGP within AS (full mesh or route reflectors)
• 10-step best path selection: Weight → Local Pref → Local Origin → AS Path → Origin → MED → eBGP/iBGP → IGP Metric → Age → Router ID
• AS_PATH provides loop prevention; LOCAL_PREF controls outbound; MED/AS_PATH prepending influences inbound
• BGP Communities enable scalable inter-AS policy signalling
• Route Reflectors scale iBGP from O(n²) to O(n)
• Default convergence is 30-90s; BFD reduces to milliseconds

**Best Practice:** Use BGP authentication, implement prefix filtering (inbound and outbound), configure BFD for sub-second convergence on critical peering sessions, and use TTL Security (GTSM) for eBGP.
troubleshooting: show ip bgp summary — Quick peer status: Established count, prefixes received, state per peer
show ip bgp [prefix] — Detailed route attributes, path selection tiebreaker steps
show ip bgp neighbors [addr] — Full session details: state, timers, capabilities, prefixes
show ip bgp neighbors [addr] received-routes — What BGP has received (requires soft-reconfiguration inbound)
show ip bgp neighbors [addr] advertised-routes — What BGP is advertising outbound
show ip bgp rib-failure — Routes BGP knows but didn't install in RIB
show ip route bgp — BGP routes in the routing table
show bgp ipv4 unicast summary — IPv4 AF-specific peer summary
debug ip bgp updates — Log BGP UPDATE messages
show ip bgp community — Inspect routes tagged with specific BGP communities
ping peer source Loopback0 — Verify TCP reachability
traceroute peer source Loopback0 — Verify multi-hop path

theory.what: HSRP and VRRP provide gateway redundancy — if the primary router fails, a backup takes over the virtual IP seamlessly. Clients never need to change their default gateway.
theory.why: A single router as default gateway is a single point of failure. FHRP ensures continuous connectivity even when a router fails — essential for high availability.
theory.how: HSRP/VRRP create a virtual IP shared between routers. Active/Master router responds to the virtual IP; Standby/Backup monitors via hello packets; if Active fails, Standby takes over (3-10 seconds). HSRP: Cisco proprietary. VRRP: Open standard (RFC 5798).
theory.when: Use FHRP whenever you have redundant routers/L3 switches serving as default gateways. Required for any HA network design.
theory.configuration:
! HSRP
interface Vlan10
 ip address 10.0.10.2 255.255.255.0
 standby 1 ip 10.0.10.1
 standby 1 priority 110
 standby 1 preempt
 standby 1 track GigabitEthernet0/0
troubleshooting: show standby
show standby brief
show vrrp
debug standby

theory.what: EtherChannel bundles multiple physical links into one logical link, providing increased bandwidth and redundancy without STP blocking the extra links.
theory.why: STP blocks redundant links. EtherChannel tricks STP into seeing multiple links as one, so all links are active. Doubles/triples bandwidth while providing failover.
theory.how: Negotiation protocols: LACP (802.3ad, open standard, preferred), PAgP (Cisco proprietary), Static (not recommended). All member links must have same speed, duplex, VLAN, and trunk settings.
theory.when: Use EtherChannel between switches, switch and server, or switch and router when more bandwidth than a single link is needed.
theory.configuration:
! LACP EtherChannel
interface range GigabitEthernet0/1-2
 channel-group 1 mode active
!
interface Port-channel1
 switchport mode trunk
troubleshooting: show etherchannel summary
show etherchannel port-channel
show lacp neighbor
show pagp neighbor

theory.what: QoS prioritizes certain traffic types over others when network congestion occurs. It ensures critical applications (voice, video) get bandwidth while less important traffic waits.
theory.why: Without QoS, all traffic is treated equally. During congestion, voice calls drop, video freezes, and critical apps slow down. QoS ensures business-critical traffic always gets through.
theory.how: QoS mechanisms: Classification (DSCP, ACL, NBAR), Marking (DSCP values), Queuing (priority queues), Scheduling (LLQ, CBWFQ), Policing/Shaping (limit bandwidth).
theory.when: Implement QoS when running VoIP, video conferencing, or any real-time application over a shared network. Also for WAN links with limited bandwidth.
theory.configuration:
! Classify and mark voice
class-map match-all VOICE
 match protocol rtp
policy-map QOS-POLICY
 class VOICE
  priority 256
 class class-default
  fair-queue
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 service-policy output QOS-POLICY
troubleshooting: show policy-map interface
show class-map
show mls qos interface
show queuing
